summary: CoAP is a RESTful protocol for constrained nodes, and basic messages work well for small payloads but sometimes larger ones are needed, such as firmware updates. This proposed standard defines block-wise transfers, which let a large resource be sent as a series of smaller blocks without needing the network to fragment packets.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending a big picture through a tiny mail slot works if you cut it into pieces and number them. This shows tiny devices how to send and receive big things in small numbered pieces.

questions: how does coap send large payloads
what is the coap block2 option
what block sizes does coap support
subtitle: How CoAP sends and receives large payloads as a series of small numbered blocks, without relying on IP fragmentation.

tldr.problem: CoAP runs over datagram transports such as UDP or DTLS, which only offer fragmentation. Fragmentation is a poor fit for constrained nodes and networks, so large payloads like firmware updates are hard to send.
tldr.mechanism: Two options, Block1 and Block2, split a request body or a response body into power-of-two sized blocks, 16 to 1024 bytes. Each block travels in its own request and response pair, and each side has a say in the block size.
tldr.outcome: A server can handle each block on its own, with no connection setup. This RFC updates RFC 7252 and was itself updated by RFC 8323.

today: RFC 7959 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7252 and has itself been updated by RFC 8323. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why CoAP Needs Block-Wise Transfers
sections.content:
CoAP brings RESTful services to constrained nodes and networks. It works hard to keep code small, messages small and requirements on the environment low. But it sits on datagram transports such as UDP or DTLS, so large resource representations run into limits: about 64 KiB for UDP, an MTU of 1280 for IPv6, and 60 to 80 bytes for 6LoWPAN adaptation-layer fragments.

Fragmentation would burden the lower layers with conversation state that is better handled in the application layer. So RFC 7959 defines a pair of Block options that move a large body across several ordinary CoAP exchanges. The overriding aim is to avoid creating conversation state at the server for block-wise GET requests.

The benefits listed include acknowledgment and individual retransmission of each block, both sides influencing the block size, easy debugging with packet tools, and random access to power-of-two sized blocks.
sections.plainLanguage: Tiny gadgets can only carry small envelopes. Instead of one huge package, they send many small envelopes, and each one gets a thank-you reply.

sections.title: The Block1 and Block2 Options
sections.content:
Block1 (option 27) refers to the payload of the request, and Block2 (option 23) refers to the payload of the response. Both are Critical options and neither may appear more than once in a message. The whole resource representation is the body; one message's content is a payload.

The option value is a 0 to 3 byte unsigned integer that packs three fields. NUM is the block number, counting from zero. M is the more bit, set when more blocks follow. SZX is a three-bit size exponent, and the block size is 2**(SZX + 4). Allowed SZX values are 0 to 6, so block sizes run from 16 to 1024 bytes. SZX value 7 is reserved: it MUST NOT be sent, and a request carrying it MUST lead to 4.00 Bad Request.

When the option is in the same message as the payload it describes (Block2 in a response, Block1 in a request), it is in descriptive usage. In the other direction it is in control usage: it asks for a specific block or states a size preference.
sections.plainLanguage: Each little envelope has a label with three things: which piece number it is, whether more pieces are coming, and how big the pieces are.

sections.title: Fetching and Sending Blocks
sections.content:
Block2 (responses). A client can suggest a size by putting Block2 with NUM 0 and M 0 on its first request. A server MUST use that size or a smaller one, and later requests MUST use the size the server actually used. Because the body may change mid-transfer, the server SHOULD include an ETag in each response and the client MUST compare ETags while reassembling. Clients SHOULD fetch all blocks without undue delay.

Block1 (requests). For PUT or POST, each response carries a Block1 option that acknowledges the block and may state the server's preferred size, which the client SHOULD follow, adjusting the block number to count in the smaller size. A server that acts only when the last block arrives answers non-final blocks with 2.31 Continue. A server that acts on every block separately may leave M unset in the response, which leaves the resource partly updated until the transfer ends.

Combinations. Block1 and Block2 can be used in one exchange. Block2 with Observe sends only the first block in a notification, and the client fetches the rest with GET requests. A multicast GET can use Block2 with NUM 0 to limit the response size.
sections.plainLanguage: The reader asks for piece after piece and can say "please make the pieces smaller". When sending, the receiver says "got it, keep going" after each piece.

sections.title: New Response Codes and Size Options
sections.content:
The RFC adds two response codes and extends one. 2.31 Continue says a block was accepted but the final outcome is not known yet. 4.08 Request Entity Incomplete says the server lacks blocks it needs, because the client did not send them all, sent them out of order, or took so long that the server discarded them. 4.13 Request Entity Too Large may now be sent at any time during a Block1 transfer, or in reply to a request without Block1 as a hint to try it.

Two elective options give size hints. Size1 (option 60) reports the size of the request representation, and Size2 (option 28) reports the size of the response representation. In a request, Size2 with value 0 asks the server for a size estimate. The end of a transfer is decided by the M bit, not by the size estimates.
sections.plainLanguage: Some messages say "keep going", "I am missing a piece" or "that is too big". Size notes just tell the other side how big the whole thing is.

sections.title: Caching and HTTP Mapping
sections.content:
Caches are free to store blocks individually or wait for the whole body. Different blocks can have different Max-Age values. A response with a block updates the freshness of the complete representation, and validating one block validates the whole.

For proxies between CoAP and HTTP, a sequence of CoAP blocks can be mapped to one HTTP transfer. The intermediary may serve later blocks from a cache, or use HTTP range requests. CoAP 4.08 maps to HTTP 408, and 4.13 maps to 413.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers in the middle can keep copies of the pieces, and can translate between the small-envelope language and the big-package language of the web.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Blocks bring several risks. Where requests are not atomic, an attacker may exploit a race condition or induce a server to use a partly updated resource. Splitting data can hide it from an Intrusion Detection System, so an IDS SHOULD implement the Block options. All blocks of a protected resource MUST be subject to the same security checks.

A stateless server could be tricked by a Block1 block with a very high block number into building a huge representation, and misleading size values could cause buffer overflows in poor implementations. Servers SHOULD avoid being exposed to resource exhaustion from state created by untrusted sources.

Block-wise transfers also reduce amplification: offering large representations only in small blocks means, for example, a 10-byte request for a 1000-byte resource yields an 80-byte response with a 64-byte block instead of 1016 bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: Because pieces arrive separately, a trickster could try to confuse the receiver. So receivers should be careful and not set aside too much space for pieces from strangers.
